text: Bloating: Abdominal bloating is a short-term disease that affects the gastrointestinal tract. Bloating is generally characterized by an excess buildup of gas, air or fluids in the stomach.
Constipation: Constipation is a bowel dysfunction that makes bowel movements infrequent or hard to pass. The stool is often hard and dry.

Diarrhoea: Diarrhea, also spelled diarrhoea, is the condition of having at least three loose, liquid, or watery bowel movements in a day. It often lasts for a few days and can result in dehydration due to fluid loss.

Dyspepsia: Indigestion, also known as dyspepsia or upset stomach, is a condition of impaired digestion. Symptoms may include upper abdominal fullness, heartburn, nausea, belching, flatulence or upper abdominal pain.
Dysphagia: Dysphagia is difficulty in swallowing. Although classified under "symptoms and signs" in ICD-10, in some contexts it is classified as a condition in its own right.
Heartburn: Heartburn is a burning sensation felt behind the breastbone. It is a symptom that is commonly linked to acid reflux and is often triggered by food.
Hematemesis: Hematemesis is the vomiting of blood. It can be confused with hemoptysis or epistaxis (nosebleed), which are more common.

Hematochezia: Hematochezia is a form of blood in stool, in which fresh blood passes through the anus while defecating. It differs from melena, which commonly refers to blood in stool originating from upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB).

Melena: Melena is a form of blood in stool which refers to the dark black, tarry feces that are commonly associated with upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The black color and characteristic strong odor are caused by hemoglobin in the blood being altered by digestive enzymes and intestinal bacteria.

Nausea: Nausea is a diffuse sensation of unease and discomfort, sometimes perceived as an urge to vomit. It can be a debilitating symptom if prolonged and has been described as placing discomfort on the chest, abdomen, or back of the throat.
Rectal discharge: Rectal discharge is intermittent or continuous expression of liquid from the anus. Normal rectal mucus is needed for proper excretion of waste.
Rectal pain: Rectal pain is the symptom of pain in the area of the rectum. A number of different causes (68) have been documented.

Regurgitation: Regurgitation or regurgitate may refer to:Regurgitation (circulation)
Regurgitation (digestion)
Regurgitate (band).
Vomiting: Vomiting is the forceful expulsion of the contents of one's stomach through the mouth and sometimes the nose. The vomited contents are known as vomit or vomitus.

Bilious vomiting of newborn: A gastrointestinal condition known as Bilious vomiting of newborn. Common presenting complaints: Vomiting. Associated symptoms: Antenatal Period: Polyhydramnios, Abdominal Distension, Lack Of Stooling. Risk factors: Unknown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Bilious vomiting of newborn differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Vomiting Of Newborn: Bilious (green/yellow) vomiting suggests intestinal obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater and is a surgical emergency; non-bilious vomiting has a broader, usually less urgent differential.

Chronic idiopathic constipation: Functional constipation, also known as chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC), is defined by less than three bowel movements per week, hard stools, severe straining, the sensation of anorectal blockage, the feeling of incomplete evacuation, and the need for manual maneuvers during feces, without organic abnormalities. Many illnesses, including endocrine, metabolic, neurological, mental, and gastrointestinal obstructions, can cause constipation as a secondary symptom. Common presenting complaints: Constipation. Associated symptoms: Hard Or Lumpy Stools, Decreased Frequency Of Bowel Movements, A Feeling Of Incomplete Evacuation Or Obstruction, Straining, Stomach Pain And Bloating. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
Chronic idiopathic constipation red flags. Red flag (RF_GI_015) triggered by complaint 'RECTAL_PAIN': Rectal bleeding or palpable mass accompanying chronic constipation.

Chronic idiopathic constipation differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Slow Transit Constipation: Chronic idiopathic constipation is a broader diagnosis of exclusion; slow transit constipation is a specific subtype confirmed by transit studies.

Constipation, unspecified: Constipation is a bowel dysfunction that makes bowel movements infrequent or hard to pass. The stool is often hard and dry. Common presenting complaints: Constipation. Associated symptoms: Infrequent Or Hard To Pass Bowel Movements, Abdominal Pain, Bloating. Risk factors: Slow Movement Of Stool Within The Colon, Irritable Bowel Syndrome, Celiac Disease, Non Celiac Gluten Sensitivity, Pelvic Floor Disorders. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Constipation, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Slow Transit Constipation: Slow transit constipation is confirmed by prolonged colonic transit time on testing; unspecified constipation has not yet been characterized by such studies. Compared to Outlet Dysfunction Constipation: Outlet dysfunction constipation involves difficulty with rectal evacuation (straining, incomplete emptying) due to pelvic floor dysfunction, typically confirmed by anorectal manometry or defecography, rather than slow colonic transit. Compared to Drug Induced Constipation: Drug-induced constipation has a clear temporal relationship to starting a constipating medication (e.g. opioids, iron, anticholinergics) and often improves on discontinuation.

Crohn's disease, unspecified, with rectal bleeding: Crohn's disease (CD) is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that may affect any segment of the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, abdominal distension, and weight loss. Common presenting complaints: Hematochezia. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Diarrhea, Abdominal Pain, Weight Loss. Risk factors: Antibiotic, Appendicitis, Tonsillectomy, Urbanity, Smoking, First Degree Relative. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
Crohn's disease, unspecified, with rectal bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_GI_002) triggered by complaint 'HEMATOCHEZIA': Ongoing or heavy rectal bleeding with dizziness/fainting.

Crohn's disease, unspecified, with rectal bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Ulcerative Colitis With Rectal Bleeding: Crohn's disease can affect any part of the GI tract with skip lesions and transmural inflammation; ulcerative colitis is continuous, limited to the colon/rectum, and mucosal only — distinguished on endoscopy and biopsy.

Functional diarrhea: A gastrointestinal condition known as Functional diarrhea. Common presenting complaints: Diarrhea. Associated symptoms: Diarrhea. Risk factors: Usually Infection (viral, Bacterial, Parasitic). Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
Functional diarrhea red flags. Red flag (RF_GI_012) triggered by complaint 'DIARRHEA': Chronic diarrhea with unexplained iron-deficiency anemia.

Functional diarrhea differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Irritable Bowel Syndrome With Diarrhea: Functional diarrhea is loose stools without associated abdominal pain meeting IBS criteria; IBS-D includes recurrent abdominal pain linked to altered bowel habit.

Functional dyspepsia: Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a common gastrointestinal disorder defined by symptoms arising from the gastroduodenal region in the absence of an underlying organic disease that could easily explain the symptoms. Characteristic symptoms include epigastric burning, epigastric pain, postprandial fullness, and early satiety. Common presenting complaints: Dyspepsia. Associated symptoms: Early Satiety, Heartburn, Nausea, Postprandial Fullness, Vomiting, And/or Epigastric Pain. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
Functional dyspepsia red flags. Red flag (RF_GI_009) triggered by complaint 'DYSPEPSIA': New dyspepsia in a patient over 50, or dyspepsia with alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia).

Functional dyspepsia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease Without Esophagitis: GERD is dominated by heartburn and acid regurgitation; functional dyspepsia presents with epigastric pain/fullness without a clear acid-reflux pattern and normal endoscopy.

Gastro-esophageal reflux disease with esophagitis, with bleeding: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) is a chronic upper gastrointestinal disease in which stomach content persistently and regularly flows up into the esophagus, resulting in symptoms and/or complications. Symptoms include dental corrosion, dysphagia, heartburn, odynophagia, regurgitation, non-cardiac chest pain, extraesophageal symptoms such as chronic cough, hoarseness, reflux-induced laryngitis, or asthma. Common presenting complaints: Heartburn. Associated symptoms: Taste Of Acid, Heartburn, Bad Breath, Chest Pain, Breathing Problems. Risk factors: Inadequate Closure Of The Lower Esophageal Sphincter. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by a group of symptoms that commonly include abdominal pain, abdominal bloating, and changes in the consistency of bowel movements. These symptoms may occur over a long time, sometimes for years. Common presenting complaints: Diarrhea. Associated symptoms: Diarrhea, Constipation, Abdominal Pain, Bloating, Abdominal Discomfort. Risk factors: Unknown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Rectal polyp: A colorectal polyp is a polyp occurring on the lining of the colon or rectum. Untreated colorectal polyps can develop into colorectal cancer. Common presenting complaints: Rectal Pain, Rectal Discharge. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
Rectal polyp red flags. Red flag (RF_GI_015) triggered by complaint 'RECTAL_DISCHARGE': Persistent rectal bleeding or discharge beyond 4-6 weeks.

Rectal polyp differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Rectal Prolapse: A rectal polyp is a discrete mucosal growth seen on endoscopy; rectal prolapse is protrusion of the full rectal wall through the anus, visible on physical exam, especially with straining.

Rectal prolapse: A rectal prolapse occurs when walls of the rectum have prolapsed to such a degree that they protrude out of the anus and are visible outside the body. However, most researchers agree that there are 3 to 5 different types of rectal prolapse, depending on whether the prolapsed section is visible externally, and whether the full or only partial thickness of the rectal wall is involved. Common presenting complaints: Rectal Pain, Rectal Discharge. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Hematemesis or melena with hemodynamic instability (dizziness, fainting, rapid heart rate) - action: call emergency services.
Large-volume or ongoing hematochezia with dizziness or fainting - action: call emergency services.
Bilious (green/yellow) vomiting in a neonate or infant - action: call emergency services.
Inability to keep any fluids down / signs of dehydration - action: go to er immediately.
Progressive dysphagia (worsening, especially to solids) with unintentional weight loss - action: urgent specialist referral.
Sudden-onset dysphagia with slurred speech, facial droop, or limb weakness - action: call emergency services.
Severe, constant, worsening abdominal pain with a rigid or distended abdomen - action: go to er immediately.
No passage of flatus or stool with abdominal distension and vomiting (suspected obstruction) - action: go to er immediately.
New-onset dyspepsia/heartburn in a patient over 50, or with alarm features - action: urgent specialist referral.
Unintentional weight loss of more than 5% body weight over 3 months - action: urgent specialist referral.
Bloody diarrhea with high fever and systemic illness (looks unwell) - action: go to er immediately.
Iron-deficiency anemia in an adult male or a postmenopausal woman without an obvious cause - action: urgent specialist referral.
Persistent vomiting for more than 24-48 hours, or vomiting with severe headache/stiff neck - action: go to er immediately.
Family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease with new bowel symptoms - action: urgent specialist referral.
Rectal mass, non-healing rectal ulcer, or persistent rectal bleeding beyond 4-6 weeks - action: urgent specialist referral.
